doc.title: Dave Brubeck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Wilton, Connecticut, November 21, 2001

title: Voice of America, Willis Conover and 'Jazz and Bones'
summary: Brubeck recalls anti-American propaganda abroad, the importance of Voice of America and Willis Conover, bootleg x-ray records, and a toast in a Polish jazz club.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: Yeah. And so was Martin Luther King. And so was Christ. And it’s gotta come from the grassroots up. And when I was in these countries I used to be appalled by the lies constantly going on the air about the United States. And right today it’s going on. There are so many great things they could say about us and show what we’re trying to do in Afghanistan, but they don’t show that. They show always the death of some children, which is terrible, and they show always the negative. We should have been investing so much — you see the Voice of America was so appreciated, but there should have been far more of that type of thing. Because I know, I’ve been to Russia three times, that at the risk of death people were listening to the Voice of America. And it came on every night out of Washington with Willis Conover. And he played mostly jazz. And the average Russian, when he speaks English, sounds like Willis Conover. And they called it “Jazz and Bones” because in the hospitals they took the plates of x-ray and they could cut a record from the broadcast, and the bones would still be seen there. And also if you were caught with one of those so-called discs, x-ray plates, that would be the end of you. Yet they took those chances, the nurses and the doctors would secretly listen. And we’ve been to secret meetings in places like Poland. The last thing they said to me, just before we came home, is we were in the basement of a hotel about 60 people in the jazz club, and one fellow stood up and said he wanted to give a toast and he said, “when you go home, remember we want freedom as much as you do.” Well, those things aren’t popular in those days. So you had to hide. And I’ve seen so many things where people were so pro- America and it was so dangerous to be.
